speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (a) whether NEA can extend the deployment of surveillance cameras beyond HDB estates to high-rise private estates to carry out enforcement against high-rise littering; and (b) whether the Ministry will amend the necessary legislation to empower NEA to do so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources whether there are effective programmes to cultivate the habit of not littering and to dispose of waste in a proper manner like that in Japan and Taiwan.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singaporeans take pride in a clean and green Singapore, and most do their part to keep the environment clean.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, there is an irresponsible minority that continues to litter and disregard prevailing societal norms.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To tackle such anti-social conduct, the National Environment Agency (NEA) has taken a tough stance on litterbugs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While enforcement may serve as a deterrent, it is not the panacea.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our primary line of defence against such behaviour should be to foster collective responsibility for our environment and cultivate positive social norms and civic mindedness among our people.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To this end, NEA and various partner organisations have been conducting campaigns and programmes to promote environmental awareness and encourage greater stewardship of our common spaces.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The annual Clean and Green Singapore (CGS) co-organised by NEA, the Public Utilities Board, the National Parks Board and the Community Development Councils encourages the community to play an active role in keeping Singapore clean and litter-free.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are also other initiatives, such as the Public Hygiene Council's annual Keep Clean, Singapore! campaign, which advocate the value of maintaining cleanliness beyond our own homes and fostering the habit of picking up after oneself.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA has also been targeting its publicity efforts at mass events, such as the National Day Parade celebrations, to remind people to pick up after themselves.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These efforts reflect the whole-of-society approach needed to keep our public spaces clean.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our national schools have also set aside time for students to clean the common areas of their school each day, and these activities have helped to inculcate values, such as a sense of responsibility and consideration for others, as well as for the environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: By starting young, these positive habits are passed down through the generations, just like in Japan today.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To the Member's question regarding littering in high-rise estates, our approach is no different.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to work with grassroots organisations and Town Councils to raise awareness about this issue amongst residents.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Home owners in private estates, therefore, have the autonomy to govern and manage the shared private spaces in a responsible manner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For this to happen, residents should come together to encourage and influence acceptable social behaviour in their communities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The management committees of these private estates can work with their residents to cultivate the right behaviour accordingly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While the Government will persist in our efforts to develop greater environmental stewardship, we cannot do this alone.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I, therefore, urge everyone to play their part in keeping Singapore a clean and green city.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The fact that NEA has committed significant resources to enforce against high-rise littering, including the deployment of surveillance cameras, rightly show that NEA and the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources are concerned about the situation of high-rise littering in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I want to ask the Senior of Minister of State: why is there a difference in the approach and actions by NEA when it comes to enforcement actions, whether it is public housing or private housing or the Executive Condominiums (EC) and the condominiums, especially where littering does pose safety concerns?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, would the Ministry keep an open mind and review the need to amend the legislation as, otherwise, NEA will have to resort to a private suit to take the culprit to task in ECs and private estates?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Private estates, such as ECs and private strata-titled condominiums, are not regarded as such a place in law, as access to such places by the public is restricted, which I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, our anti-littering law, therefore, does not apply to littering within these private estates, such as condominiums.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But having said that, many condominiums already have by-laws that prohibit littering within their estates.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The management committee of these private estates can actually work with the residents to encourage and influence the right behaviour accordingly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While the process may be challenging, MCSTs can, nonetheless, turn to this option if all other means, like reaching out to the errant residents, fail, including even community mediation, for instance.
